person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: what the COVID-19 pandemic did to the mental health of undergraduates at one large university, asked in a semistructured interview a month after the state stay-at-home order
span.quote: We then elicited pandemic-specific stressors and their manifestations across 12 academic-, health-, and lifestyle-related categories of outcomes such as effects on own or loved ones’ health, sleeping habits, eating habits, financial situation, changes to their living environment, academic workload, and social relations. Students were also asked about the impact of COVID-19 on depressive and suicidal thoughts. These constructs were derived from existing literature identifying prominent factors affecting college students’ mental health [20,21].

span.label: which pandemic stressors students report, how severely each affects them, and why so few used the counselling service available to them
span.quote: Third, although a vast majority of participants answered that they have not used the university counseling service during the pandemic, only a few of them provided reasons.

span.label: an interview survey of undergraduates during the pandemic peak, carrying both a literature-derived twelve-category severity rating and an open thematic coding of the same transcripts
span.quote: A single coder (CS), trained in qualitative analysis methods, analyzed the transcripts and identified themes using an open coding process, which does not use a priori codes or codes created prior to the analysis and places an emphasis on information that can be extracted directly from the data.

span.label: existence

span.label: student distress during a pandemic, recorded through two instruments at once - one whose categories were fixed by earlier papers and one with no categories at all
span.quote: We then elicited pandemic-specific stressors and their manifestations across 12 academic-, health-, and lifestyle-related categories of outcomes such as effects on own or loved ones’ health, sleeping habits, eating habits, financial situation, changes to their living environment, academic workload, and social relations. span.label: semistructured Zoom interviews by 20 trained undergraduate researchers, transcribed by an AI service and manually verified, with PSS-10 scores, a four-point severity rating over twelve categories, and open thematic coding by a single coder reviewed by two others
span.term: semistructured Zoom interviews by 20 trained undergraduate researchers, transcribed by an AI service and manually verified, with PSS-10 scores, a four-point severity rating over twelve categories, and open thematic coding by a single coder reviewed by two others
span.quote: The interviews were conducted by 20 undergraduate researchers trained in qualitative methods and the use of the interview survey guide described above. None of the authors conducted the interviews. All interviews were conducted via Zoom [22] and were audio recorded. The recordings were later transcribed using Otter.ai [23], an artificial intelligence–based transcription service, and verified for accuracy manually.

span.label: the same interviews are read twice - once against twelve categories written by earlier papers and rated 0 to 3, once with no categories at all. Whatever the open coding surfaces that the twelve do not contain is a direct measurement of what the literature's vocabulary could not see. THE COMPARISON IS AVAILABLE IN THIS PAPER AND IS NOT DRAWN
span.term: two apertures on one set of transcripts
span.quote: We then elicited pandemic-specific stressors and their manifestations across 12 academic-, health-, and lifestyle-related categories of outcomes such as effects on own or loved ones’ health, sleeping habits, eating habits, financial situation, changes to their living environment, academic workload, and social relations. Students were also asked about the impact of COVID-19 on depressive and suicidal thoughts. These constructs were derived from existing literature identifying prominent factors affecting college students’ mental health [20,21].

span.label: open coding without a priori codes means the themes are whatever a trained reader sees. One person did all of it; two others were brought in afterwards to resolve discrepancies and discuss saturation. That is a review, not an independent coding, and no agreement statistic is available because none could be computed
span.term: the coder is the instrument, and there was one
span.quote: A single coder (CS), trained in qualitative analysis methods, analyzed the transcripts and identified themes using an open coding process, which does not use a priori codes or codes created prior to the analysis and places an emphasis on information that can be extracted directly from the data.

span.label: the interviews were run by 20 trained undergraduate researchers and none of the authors conducted one. That removes the authors' expectations from the elicitation and introduces twenty different interviewing styles into it - a trade the design makes deliberately and the paper reports plainly
span.term: twenty interviewers, none of them the authors
span.quote: The interviews were conducted by 20 undergraduate researchers trained in qualitative methods and the use of the interview survey guide described above. None of the authors conducted the interviews. All interviews were conducted via Zoom [22] and were audio recorded. The recordings were later transcribed using Otter.ai [23], an artificial intelligence–based transcription service, and verified for accuracy manually.

span.label: recordings were transcribed by an AI service and verified for accuracy manually. The qualitative data is therefore a machine's reading of speech, corrected - and what a correction pass catches is a different set from what it misses
span.term: a transcript produced by a machine and checked by hand
span.quote: The interviews were conducted by 20 undergraduate researchers trained in qualitative methods and the use of the interview survey guide described above. None of the authors conducted the interviews. All interviews were conducted via Zoom [22] and were audio recorded. The recordings were later transcribed using Otter.ai [23], an artificial intelligence–based transcription service, and verified for accuracy manually.

span.label: participants were also asked to describe stressors, coping strategies and barriers in a typical semester WITHOUT associating them with the pandemic. The within-person baseline is collected from the same person in the same sitting, which controls for who is answering and not for when they are answering
span.term: a non-pandemic comparison inside the same interview
span.quote: Third, participants were guided to describe stressors, coping strategies, and barriers to mental health treatment during a typical semester without associating with the COVID-19 pandemic.

span.label: the sample is small compared with survey-only studies, traded for elaboration and clarifying detail
span.quote: First, the sample size for our interview survey was relatively small compared to typical survey-only studies; however, the survey interview approach affords the capture of elaboration and additional clarifying details, and therefore complements the survey-based approaches of prior studies focusing on student mental health during this pandemic [10,11,50].

span.label: the sample is from one large university and may not generalize to all college students
span.quote: Second, the sample used is from one large university, and findings may not generalize to all college students.

span.label: a majority of participants were engineering majors; a stratified nationwide sample across wider disciplines is needed to verify and amend the findings
span.quote: Additionally, a majority of our participants were from engineering majors. Therefore, future work is needed to use a stratified nationwide sample across wider disciplines to verify and amend these findings.

span.label: almost none of the participants who had not used the counselling service gave a reason, so the study's central practical question is left open
span.quote: Third, although a vast majority of participants answered that they have not used the university counseling service during the pandemic, only a few of them provided reasons.

span.label: mental health problems were not analysed by demographic characteristics or by personal and social context
span.quote: Finally, we did not analyze how student mental health problems differ by demographic characteristics (eg, age, gender, academic year, major) or other personal and social contexts (eg, income, religion, use of substances).

span.label: multiple analyses of the collected data are still in progress; only the PSS results and COVID-19-related findings appear here
span.quote: Although multiple analyses of the collected data are currently under progress, PSS results and the COVID-19–related findings are presented in this paper.

span.quote: Participants were recruited by undergraduate student researchers through email, text messaging, and snowball sampling.
